Alfred Stieglitz. An American photographer and tastemaker who championed photography as a fine art in the early twentieth century. Through his galleries, journals, and exhibitions, he promoted both his own work and that of peers like Georgia O'Keeffe, establishing photography's legitimacy alongside painting and sculpture.

Stieglitz ran Gallery 291 in New York from 1905 to 1917, the first major gallery dedicated to photography and avant-garde modern art. There he showcased works not only by photographers but also by painters including Picasso, Rodin, and Cézanne. He edited and published two influential journals: Camera Notes, from 1897 to 1902, and Camera Work, from 1903 to 1917. These reproduced fine photographic prints alongside essays arguing for photography's artistic merit against those who dismissed it as merely mechanical.

In 1907 Stieglitz photographed The Steerage, a composition of passengers on a ship's deck arranged in geometric patterns. He called it his masterpiece, and it became an icon of photography as visual poetry rather than mere documentation. He pioneered pictorialism initially, with its soft focus and romantic sensibility, but then shifted toward modernist abstraction and pure photography—crisp focus, strong geometric compositions, rejecting the romanticism he had once embraced.

Stieglitz married Georgia O'Keeffe and created a famous series of intimate photographs of her that blurred boundaries between portraiture, abstraction, and sexuality, challenging conventions of the medium. He shares a deep artistic legacy with later photographer Ansel Adams, who credited Stieglitz's advocacy for photography's artistic legitimacy as foundational to his own career. Henri Cartier-Bresson's philosophy of the decisive moment also reflected Stieglitz's influence on treating photography as a form of visual poetry.
